nameStory: The Sword-bearing Conehead gets its dramatic name from the sharp, blade-like projection at the tip of its cone-shaped head, which really does look like a tiny sword! The 'conehead' part refers to the distinctive pointed shape of its head that extends forward beyond its eyes, making it look like it's wearing a medieval helmet.
description: The Sword-bearing Conehead is a slender, green katydid with an unmistakable pointed head that extends forward like a cone. These elegant insects are typically bright green with long, thread-like antennae and powerful hind legs built for jumping. They're medium-sized for katydids, with females being noticeably larger than males, and their wings extend well beyond their body when folded.

idTips.label: Sword-like head projection
idTips.description: The head extends forward in a sharp, pointed cone with a blade-like tip that feels firm to the touch - this is the diagnostic 'sword' feature

idTips.label: Bright green coloration
idTips.description: Body is typically vibrant grass-green, sometimes with subtle yellow tones, helping it blend perfectly with vegetation

idTips.label: Long, delicate antennae
idTips.description: Thread-thin antennae are longer than the body and constantly move as the insect explores its surroundings

idTips.label: Extended wing tips
idTips.description: Wings fold along the back and extend noticeably beyond the end of the abdomen, creating a sleek silhouette

idTips.label: Powerful jumping legs
idTips.description: Hind legs are thick and muscular with spiny surfaces that feel rough when handled gently

habitat: Look for Sword-bearing Coneheads in tall grasses, weedy fields, and meadow edges throughout New England's lowlands and foothills. They prefer areas with dense herbaceous growth like goldenrod patches, unmowed field margins, and prairie-like openings where they can easily move through the vegetation canopy.

seasonality.spring: Adults are not yet active; eggs are overwintering in plant stems and soil.
seasonality.summer: Young nymphs begin appearing in mid-summer, looking like miniature wingless versions of adults with the same distinctive pointed heads.
seasonality.fall: Peak activity period when adults are fully developed, actively singing, mating, and most easily found in tall grass and weedy areas.
seasonality.winter: Adults die after first hard frost; eggs remain dormant in vegetation and will hatch the following year.

funFact: Male Sword-bearing Coneheads are accomplished musicians who create their chirping songs by rubbing their wings together like tiny violins, and they can actually adjust the pitch and volume of their calls based on background noise levels - essentially turning up their 'stereo' when it gets too noisy!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other conehead katydids, but the Sword-bearing's head projection comes to a sharp point like a blade, while Round-tipped Coneheads have blunt, rounded head tips. Memory trick: 'Sword' = sharp point, 'Round' = blunt tip.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'katydids,' coneheads like this species don't actually make the classic 'katy-did' sound - that's produced by their broad-winged cousins in the true katydid group. Coneheads produce more of a continuous buzzing or trilling sound instead.
compareHints: Among New England's coneheads, the Sword-bearing is distinguished by its sharp, blade-like head tip, while the Round-tipped Conehead has a blunt, rounded projection and the Robust Conehead is noticeably bulkier overall. The Sword-bearing also tends to be more commonly found in drier, weedy habitats compared to some of its moisture-loving relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's conehead katydids, the round-tipped species stands out for its distinctly blunt head cone, while most relatives like the sword-bearing conehead have sharp, pointed tips.
